title: Great Rice Cooker! If you are into good quality rice
body:
This is a great rice cooker! I had a $400 Japanese one for five years before I switched to this one. This uses real pressure to cook the rice, so the rice is cooked much faster. My previous one took minimum of 35 min for fast cooking (white rice), and at least 45 for normal cooking (white rice). This one only takes 15 min for fast, and 30 min for normal cooking. I am very happy with the cooker. However, the rice seems to be more sticky due to the cooking method, so I had to try out several different method (water volume, setting, etc) to find the rice I want.
When I received the product, the inner pot was scratched and the steam plate was missing (sold by Amazon.com LLC). I contacted CuckooWorld.com to get a new inner pot and steam plate, since I did not want to return the whole thing. The representatives were very courteous, and while it was a little bit of a hassle to get them replaced, they finally shipped them out. Overall, nice experience and I would definitely recommend this to anyone who likes good quality rice.

author: Otterindawata
title: Updated review
body:
It's Beautiful! This rice cooker has an excellent sturdy pot with lots of room for larger rice batches. I generally use about 3 gou a day which is above the 2 gou minimum cook of this unit. The voice is quite cute but I prefer that this machine works in stealth mode. Though the price is steep and the instruction manual looks to be done by google translate the simplicity and direct nature works wonderfully. This item is quite large in comparison to the actual cooking pot. As far as cleaning is concerned I'm going to handwash everything with a sponge to protect the coatings.
Update=> I've used this for steel cut oats, and it works WONDERFULLY. 1 gou of steel cut oats and this puppy had everything tasting perfectly after 80 minutes. I used to cook these in a slow cooker overnight but this cooker pushed out a wonderfully textured steel cut oats batch with ease. I will note that you should dial the amount of oats in for your intended texture. For my next batch I will probably use more oats per minimum fill in order to get firmer oats but the increase won't be more than 1/8 of a gou ( a couple tablespoons).
UPDATE TO THE UPDATE... So YEAH the oats decided to get messy and slimy completely clogging the dewtray.. so the oat cooking days have ended. However sushi rice, mixed beans and rice, bread proofing.... AMAZING. I will say that though cleaning the nooks and crannies can be tiresome the quality of cooking pays into profits... I am so very glad I made this investment.

title: Comparison of 3Cup & 6Cup
body:
I love this one —its luxurious color, elegant design, and incredible price.
Thirteen years ago, I spent about $500 in my Cuckoo 6-cup rice cooker, which has served me well every day over the years, consistently making great rice for my family. Now that my children have left home, my husband and I want a smaller cooker for fresh, daily rice, so I picked for this  3-cup model.

I have always believed in the value of Cuckoo, even at a higher price. The current model is available at an excellent price, especially considering that six years ago, a 3-cup Cuckoo for my kids was priced at $450.

If you cook rice occasionally for friends and family, a 6-cup or larger model might be best. But for everyday use by one or two people, the 3-cup model is ideal.

I took photos comparing my old 6-cup and the new 3-cup. While the exterior size of the 3-cup is slightly smaller, its inner pot is definitely more compact.

I’ll keep my old 6-cup unit for holiday gatherings while enjoying my new 3-cup every day.

author: Helen
title: Review after 5 years daily use; how to replace inner pot/gasket
body:
Initially purchased this around 2018. It's not perfect, but is the best out of all the rice cooker I've tested. Jump to the end of the review if you just want to know about replacing the inner pot/gasket.

This size is perfect for singles/couples. I live alone, and make 3 cups of rice every other day. After I make rice, I leave it on keep warm mode in perpetuity - so that I have access to warm rice at a moment's notice.

It's got lots of features, but it doesn't really matter to me. I only use it to make short grain white rice (Korean/Japanese "sticky" rice). I have also used a cheaper non-pressure Cuckoo rice cooker in the past. It's ok, but the rice doesn't come out as soft due to lack of pressure, which is very important to me.

I have also tried a Zojirushi pressure rice cooker. It made comparable rice, BUT the stainless lid started to RUST within few days of use. It's probably fine if you are a normal person that occasionally eat rice, and don't leave it on warm mode all the time. To me, this was a dealbreaker.

After 2 years of using the Cuckoo every day, the inner pot started to peel, and moisture would collect inside the rice cooker, due to the aging of the rubber gasket.

This is expected.

Replacement inner pot can be found on ebay, for about $60. The rubber gasket (called "packing") for about $20. With international shipping from Korea, it'll run you about $90-$100 in total.

Search for the model number EHSS0309F, or the Korean equivalent EHS0320F (same rice cooker, just different voltage). The rubber gasket ("packing") model is CCP-DP03.

Make sure to replace BOTH the inner pot and the rubber gasket. Otherwise, the steam will continue to leak.

So, you can expect to spend $100 in replacement parts every 2 years if you use the rice cooker every day like me. To me, this is worth every penny, but may not be the right choice for everyone.

author: Tristan
title: Not just a rice cooker
body:
Many of you might be wondering if there is any sense in buying $400~$500 rice cookers. Especially since rice costs so little and is usually not the main dish everyone looks forward to eating. It might make less sense and thus might be harder to justify the cost for the ones that don't eat rice regularly. However, for those that do eat rice on a regular basis, and especially for those that enjoy eating sticky short-grain rice instead of the dry long-grain ones you can find in American supermarkets, investing in a quality rice cooker makes much more sense.

Even though rice is never the main dish on the table (with the exception for when you make rice dishes like fried rice, bibimbap, etc), having quality rice is still very important for elevating the overall dining experience. In my opinion, having quality rice is really important because of how it compliments so many other dishes (especially the Asian dishes). Imagine eating a really good pork belly kimchi stew but only having mediocre flaky rice to go with it instead of fresh steaming sticky rice cooked to perfection.

Good rice cookers not only cook the rice perfectly but they also keep the rice fresh for a lot longer, preventing it from getting all mushy shortly after cooking it like they usually do with cheap rice cookers. This is convenient because then you don't have to cook rice every time you eat to have fresh rice; the 3 day old rice in these quality rice cookers will still taste fresh thanks to its induction heating technology.

These are the two things I look for when I buy new rice cookers: Pressure Cooking & Induction Heating. Pressure cooking is how the rice cooker ensures your rice cooks perfectly and gets all gelatinous while keeping the cooking time super short. Induction heating is how the rice cooker keeps the cooked rice fresh for longer. Usually, rice cookers that have both features will run expensive, like this model does. In my opinion, the extra cost is worth it. Additionally, rice cookers that has both IH and Pressure Cooking are built with quality materials to give consumers the premium experience.

Lastly, don't view these premium rice cookers as being simple kitchen appliances used for cooking rice and rice only. They have so many other ways they can be utilized!

PS - You guys are probably confused as to why the content of my review doesn't match with the rating I'm giving this product. Well,  I knocked two stars off because I received a used product. I'm going to get it replaced but everything I said about this product still stands. Oh, and I also received a different color with the one I received being silver.

author: Tuckers Kahuna
title: Makes the best rice I've ever had.
body:
The rice cooker I've been using started to burn the bottom of the rice, and I realized that I've had it for almost 25 years!  So I thought I'd treat myself to a super nice cooker this time, and I found this on sale. Maybe it will last another 25 years!

The Cuckoo is a bit cuckoo to setup. It's very complicated and weird, but worth the effort. I love the quality of rice it makes, whether it's long grain Thai basmati, or short grain Japanese style, it comes out delicious.  I am using a water ratio of about 1.9x water to rice for most rice.  Short grain brown rice  also came out good with a bit more water added. I also tried the germinated brown rice recipe.  I gotta say though, the texture and taste of that was not much different than regular brown rice cooking, so not worth the extra effort for me.

I like short grain 'kokari' style japanese rice the best, but with this cooker I've liked all types I have tried. I've seen reviews saying that Cuckoo doesn't do as well with long grain rice, but I LOVE the long grain rice I've made in it even more than short grain.  Even tho I'm not a big fan of brown rice, it's nearly as good as white in the Cuckoo so I will be eating more of it.  I have even tried a wild rice blend, and that was excellent.  I do tend to like stickier rice, probably more towards the Korean than Japanese style and the Cuckoo delivers.

One of the reasons I got this cooker is the size, as a single person, I don't need a lot of rice.  And I typically use a 1/4 cup of dried rice to make a single portion.  This takes about 13 minutes on turbo mode or about 22 minutes on regular. So super quick and easy.  I have also found that larger portions take only a bit more time.  My experience with previous cookers is that doubling the size of the portion will usually double the time.  Not with the Cuckoo, it only adds 10-25% of the time.

I was really skeptical of the auto-clean feature, but it actually works extremely well.  I clean out  the bowl, wipe down the upper lid and run it, and the whole unit comes out very clean.  I have made some recipes with a bit more ingredients and found that the insides do 'gum up' a bit more, and removing the top lid and cleaning it is essential.  Running the auto-clean twice made it sparkling after that.  My one irritation is that its hard to remove the top inner lid.  It's really clamped down and I have to work hard to get it off.  Could be a challenge for someone with arthritis or mobility issues.  Sometimes I've had to use a pair of pliers.

The voice guide is essential because it's so complicated.  And I find the voice funny to hear.  It talks so much and unnecessarily.  It will announce it's going into sleep mode, for instance. Why would I need to know that?

My only negatives for this cooker is the price, the size which is large for how small the portion of rice it makes, the weight, it's something like 12 lbs, so hard to move around.  And the difficulty in removing the inner lid, that is irritating.

author: Dino Sarma
title: 4 stars with reservations
body:
The turbo mixed rice setting is perfect for Jasmine rice and other long grain rices. The glutinous rice regular setting works well for sushi rice, and the glutinous rice turbo setting works well for sona masoori and ponni rice. I have yet to try actual glutinous rice, but will update once I do. Basmati rice does well in the mixed rice turbo setting. Parboiled long grain rice works well in the glutinous rice regular setting. Parboiled basmati does well with the mixed rice turbo setting. The brown rice setting has worked well for brown basmati, brown long grain, brown Jasmine, and brown sushi rice. I do err on the side of adding slightly more water than the cooker calls for. If you forget to soak your brown rice overnight (it produces a softer brown rice which is less challenging to chew), you can use the GABA rice setting, and you'll get the same effect. It takes a couple hours, but it makes a brown rice that doesn't taste like health food.

To access the turbo setting when you're making something, hit the start button twice. While the rice is cooking, there will be multiple times that the cooker will tell you it's doing something. Before it starts venting out the steam (it is a pressure cooker after all), it gives you a heads-up. If you don't like to use the microwave to reheat something, the multi cook function hit for 10 minutes will get your wet food (soup, stew, beans, etc) from fridge cold to nice and hot.

What the superpower that this rice cooker has over larger models is sheer /speed/. I can wash off some rice, hit the glutinous rice turbo setting, and it'll be done /from start to finish/ in 12 - 16 minutes, depending on how much rice is in there. This isn't 12 minutes from when it hits pressure. This isn't 12 minutes from after it comes to a boil. This is where I hit start, and the cooker starts timing 12 minutes. When that timer has run out, the rice is ready, period. If you're impatient like me, add about 1/3 cup extra water to the mix, and you won't have to let the rice sit there and redistribute for 10 minutes after the cooking is done. The rice will be on the slightly softer side, but that's not entirely a bad thing, in my opinion. I don't care for rice that's too hard.

The self cleaning function is where this guy really shines. There's been times where I'll cook something, and the top plate gets this starchy film all over it, and I don't want to spend all day cleaning it. The auto clean loosens up any stuck on food bits from the inner pot, and the lid, so that you can easily wipe it off.

This isn't a small appliance though. Even though it's a 3 cup, the body is still fairly bulky. As counter top footprint goes, it's on par with my air fryer. That said, because I use it so much, it's worth it for me. I like the smaller size, because it keeps me from making too much of something, and having leftovers forever. I don't mind a leftover that I can clear off in one or two meals, but much more than that, and I'll get bored. I live alone, and it's easy to make too much of something, and then never want to eat it again, because you've had it twice a day five days in a row.

title: Adorable and Efficient Little Cooker! 🍚💕
body:
Oh my goodness, the CUCKOO CRP-EHSS0309FG 3-Cup Induction Heating Pressure Rice Cooker is just the cutest addition to my kitchen! I mean, who knew a rice cooker could be so adorable and efficient at the same time?

First of all, let's talk about the size. It's perfect for my smaller kitchen and doesn't take up too much counter space. The compact design is like a tiny kitchen companion that's always ready to whip up a delicious batch of rice for me.

The induction heating and pressure cooking combo is like a magic spell for rice. It cooks it to perfection every single time! Fluffy, aromatic, and oh-so-tasty. And let's not forget about the "keep warm" function, which comes in handy when I get lost in the world of cute cat videos and forget about my cooking.

But wait, the cuteness factor doesn't stop there! The soft chime that plays when the rice is ready is like music to my ears. It's like my little rice cooker is announcing, "Ta-da! Your meal is served!" I can't help but giggle every time I hear it.

Cleaning up is a breeze too. The non-stick interior makes sure rice doesn't stick around where it's not wanted, and a quick wipe is all it takes to keep my little cooker sparkling clean.

Overall, the CUCKOO CRP-EHSS0309FG has stolen my heart. It's not just a kitchen appliance; it's a cute, reliable, and efficient rice-making companion. If you're looking for a small rice cooker with a big personality, this one's a winner! 🍚💕

author: D. Zebrowski
title: Always told an Asian rice maker is best, makes sense, and this agrees. Cuckoo!
body:
I mean, surely in Asia they are among the chief consumers of rice as the center of their diet, where we here in the US tend more toward potatoes, primarily. I probably eat fries 5-10x more than I do rice, and that number is likely considerably higher.

In truth, I think aside from convenience, one of the main reasons this is the case is that rice in the US, outside of an Asian restaurant, simply isn't very good. I mean, it's alright, not bad at all. Yet in truth, easily the best rice I ever eat is in a Japanese restaurant, Chinese following closely behind in my own culinary experiences.

As such, I indeed had often heard that if I ever really wanted a proper rice maker, I would do best to purchase one actually manufactured and made for an Asian audience, even if it meant having to deal with foreign controls.

Thankfully, with this premium rice maker and from a brand well known to be a rice cooking leader, they also included an option for English speech. Wow, so thankful! Kind of scary to get it to turn on, but with a few guesses, in the end, just push the buttons named in the fairly obscure manual, get it to selection 3, and English will greet you from then on.

So, to the actual review.

First, this rice maker is simply solid. Premium to be certain. I've used a few rice makers in recent years of varying quality, and this is hands down the best by a country mile. Landslide victory, not only in its build and controls, but most importantly, in the rice it produces.

I consider is fairly obvious, but I'll take a moment to point it out anyway, that this is a pressure cooker, outright. It has a whole design around producing the best rice in quite a variety of iterations, but when it comes down to it, what makes it extra special is that it can make a premium quality batch of rice in about 15 minutes. Huge bonus points and bragging rights.

Think of it as an instant pot, yet made specifically for rice, only (with a few exceptions, or additions. "Multi-cook" is the generic cook function on the device.

The controls are a but daunting to learn, with all of the options. Yet I so thoroughly enjoy the Asian cultural norms, the bright and peppy messages, the built in humor. All quite fun and uplifting to me. Once you get your feet wet, it's actually quite simple, all in all.

Perhaps one of the most important questions for me, as to whether or not this device would really see much counter time was the cleaning. Would it be easy, or a complicated process? Well, both primary ways for cleaning are so super simple.

One, the bowl within is so well made, the surface so non-stick, that cleaning it after a batch takes almost no time at all by hand. The second way is to use the cleaning cycle, which is also super simple and easy. Drop some water to the mark, push the button, and 15 minutes or so later, all done. Sanitized.

The first batch of rice was better than any I had made in years, and believe me, I have tried a ridiculous number of methods and means. It was easy, and super quick. White rise, turbo. Super sticky, yet not the least bit "glommy". Yum. Had such a good dish of Gen. Tsao chicken. Wonderful.

So, in the end, if you like rice and want the best, or simply want to have a premier rice maker, this is easily an option for the top of the list, and I mean for rice makers world-wide.

Ultimately, and according to wisdom and expectation, those who eat rice the most have also perfected the maker thereof. I am very thankful to have it, and look forward to all of my future rice dishes simply being terrific.

title: One of my best kitchen appliances
body:

Will be getting other rices and enjoying them in this cooker as well.  Everything is marked just add the number of cups of rice using the enclosed rice measuring cup and add water to the matching cup line.  Then close and lock the lid and select the type of rice being cooked.  Everything is automated and it voices what is happening during the cooking process.  The most difficult item for me was getting it set to English not knowing what the directions meant by "Standby mode".  Standby mode is when all the indicators go out when sitting a long time.  The 3 language options are Korean, English, and Chinese. with the default option being Korean.
Cleanup is easy with this cooker as all the items needing washed are easily removed for cleaning and it has a setting for sterilization cleaning.  Will also be trying some of the slow-cook meal options.

date: Reviewed in the United States on May 23, 2024
author: AnonyAr
title: I love rice!
body: I'm one of those people that grew up with a rice cooker, but was never taught how it could be used it for more than just rice, it was just known and never acknowledged. Growing up, they were all pretty basic, to middle of the road, type of rice cookers, most of which have the electric plate heating and a variety of different types of stainless steel, aluminum, or non-stick coated pans.I've always wanted one of those fancy rice cookers that talks, has all kinds of sound effects, music  and/or talks to you, and I grabbed this mostly because I wanted to see if there really is a big difference between the ones I've mentioned vs one that costs 3-5x more than some rice cookers, and has induction, and/or pressure cooking features.Straight out of the box, it has this beautiful, brushed copper finish, black and silver details all around. On top of that it has backlit wording, a inset lit screen for the time notifications, lock and unlock dial, a pressure release valve and more. I greatly appreciate the fact that the inside plate on the top, as well as the pressure valve casing comes off, and there is a water dispenser on the back side , for easy cleaning. The cooking pot/bowl has sturdy plastic handles, which are easy to the touch when the rest of the pot is hot. The inside of the bowl is coated and has all kinds of indication lines for anything you can think of. Seriously, this thing is a tank and it's super bougie. Like so fancy, with so many details and features, I feel like I shouldn't have it in my possession.My first dish would naturally be rice, to get a good baseline, but I decided to go hard and made Filipino porridge called Lugaw, which I normally cook on the stove in under an hour. I checked the recipe in the given manual, to get an idea of ratios needed and used that mostly as a guide since lugaw contains some other ingredients than a standard chicken porridge, plus I wanted to make double the amount. The measuring cup included, doesn't have ccs noted for liquid measure, so I had to do a quick conversion of 1.23cups, that equates to 300cc of water/broth. Thankfully the rice bowl also has liquid lines noted inside too, but I still felt like I had a little bit less water than I should've used. Either way, I set it all and forgot it. About an hour later, it sounded off like a choo choo, indicating it was releasing steam and soon let me know it was time. I opened up the rice cooker, and it was magic. I mixed everything around, everything was evenly cooked, and nothing was burned one bit! Did I need more liquid? Not really, the rice cooker just knew. I actually like my lugaw thicker, but could easily add more broth to make it a little lighter, thinner, and soupy.Honestly, I've looked high and low, for videos and data on induction cooking rice makers like this and the reasons why this costs that much and I'm still trying to figure that out, as every video I saw gave the basics, and those on the tubes just made rice with no clear data, or idea on how to review a rice cooker. I'm not saying this will be #1 review, but I'm trying. The big things the company advertises is that this one provides a higher pressure than most, and it has induction heating, which ensures more even cooking. My mother is convinced that it eliminates starch, but that's a high claim and I'm not a believer in that so much, with any type of rice cooker. The options and guidance are definitely a big plus with this, and I plan on making it my right hand man in the kitchen next to the air fryer, since time and energy is so limited when it comes to making meals up to 2-3 times a day. On top of that, it makes just enough food for 2 people, and has some leftover for the next day compared to my slow cooker that can take all day, and up to 8 hours for one meal, and more leftovers than my freezer can handle!Honestly, this guy is not necessary if you plan on using a rice cooker like this JUST to make rice, but I have seen lower level models with the same, or similar features from this company at big box warehouses. This is really the bougie version of certain models with all the fancy details, mechanics, and look. Plus it's a beast compared to my other 6 cup rice cooker, so you'll also have to accommodate for the size in your kitchen. Think deep, not wide. Either way, I'm totally keeping this since I plan to make it more of an everyday appliance, compared to my other rice cooker that just takes a nap in the cupboard and comes out to play once a week. Try it if you must, but know if you pay the price, appliances like these are more of an investment.

date: Reviewed in the United States on May 21, 2024
author: Cheryl
title: The manual is confusing, disorganized and has tiny print but it makes great congee!
body: The white rice is clumpy despite rinsing it until completely clear.  The brown rice was best but I realized I used the wrong water line and used less water.I also made Gaba rice which turned out good, it was slightly clumpy although the texture was good after adding butter.  After some googling, I found out that after you soak the rice for 16 hours, the Gaba process sprouts the rice during a 2-hour process and the last hour cooks the rice.But even the Gaba rice was slightly clumpy.  I did let the rice rest for 10 mins this time and it was better.I had to start highlighting sections of the manual so I could find the scattered information.  Page 17 is very important because it is there that it tells you the water line to use for Brown Rice.  There is a small tidbit about the Direct Touch menus but there is no title to grab your attention and the print is so tiny it??s easy to miss.  There is no mention of the steam plate.To start, there is a MODE button and a Selection dial and the voice helps you along, thankfully.  When you turn her on, she is speaking Korean, so I was in a bit of a panic but it was easy to use the Mode function to set to English AND to set the time.I focused on cooking rice and ignored setting up timers for reheating and warming, and the My Mode feature, until I am comfortable with the settings.I tested how well it cooks rice by making medium grain brown rice.  Each grain was perfectly cooked despite using less water.  Then I tried white jasmine rice, which turned out very clumpy, even though I had rinsed it until the water was super clear.I wanted to use the steamer plate.  No where in the manual does it say anything about steaming.  There??s a Multi-Cook function but the only thing it mentions is how to change the preset time of the Multi-Cook function. I contacted support for this reason and they sent me a PDF manual that has a different recipe table than what is in the manual that came with my machine.  So again, the manual is lacking.The 6-cup unit is a little over 14 inches in depth but the feet sit approximately 10 inches apart.  It??s not terribly heavy, so easy to move around.  The cord is located on the left side and fairly short.  The cup markings inside are white which makes them easy to see, which I love. One side is Korean, the other side is printed in English.There is no way to turn off the unit, which bugs me but it does turn to power save modeTo make rice on any of the Direct Touch selections, merely add rice and then add water to the correct line and then touch your selection.  Brown rice you must also use the Gaba line. I??m a bit disappointed as I make better rice on the stove-top.  I am still researching to see if I'm missing something.

author: Iphone user
title: A significant improvement over older rice cookers
body:
My family eats rice at least 5 days a week and we are loving this rice cooker.  We came from a 10 year old Zojirushi (non-induction) which is already a good rice cooker however I was really surprised at the improvements this model offered.

The best improvement is that the pressure cooking makes the rice firm and fluffy at the same time.  With the right amount of water dialed in, the rice has a wonderful texture and mouth feel.
Second since it uses pressure, the cooking time is drastically reduced.  A 45minute wait is now down to 26 minutes for 3 servings!  The machine can tell how much rice is inside and displays an estimate as soon as you press the cook button.  It also talks to you in English, Korean or Chinese.

We have made long grain jasmine and calrose rice with this and both produce rice that is a significant improvement over our old rice cooker.
There are all sorts of presets for mixed rice, brown rice, and steamer and porridge functions which we rarely use but it's there.  There is also a customized rice cooking program where you can dial in exactly how you want the rice to turn out.

The price of this rice cooker is significant.. however for an appliance which will be used almost everyday, I believe it is well worth the time savings and most importantly, the improvement in texture you will get.

author: Wonderwater
title: Caution: EP7 error with this rice cooker
body:
Like others said, this unit has EP7 error issue. This error is related to the temperature sensor and has to be fixed by sending the unit to a Cuckoo service center. This error happened around 4-5 years after the 1-year warranty expired, which means all the shipping and repair costs are on the consumers. I bought this cooker for over 4 years but lightly used for about 2-3 years. Then suddenly last week the EP7 error occurred. As I purchased the cooker for over $600 on Amazon, it would really be a bummer to throw it away. So I chose to send it to the service to have it fixed for the sake of the amount of money I already spent on it. I am still waiting for the service center to let me know how much the cost would be after they check my cooker, but others said it costed them $100 or so.

I am really disappointed for the quality considering the premium price I paid for it. I have one Zojirushi rice cooker for over 10 years which costed less than 1/3 of this Cuckoo cooker and I am still using it. So if I could make a different choice again 4 years ago, I could have bought the Zojirushi IH cooker. It is so unfortunate that Cuckoo would charge customers to fix this known issue. It probably explained why the price of this cooker decreased from $600 to $400 now. So if you are considering buying a new rice cooker, probably think about what you are getting into. If you look for something with longevity, this model is not the one.

author: Ree Méndez
title: Induction Heating Pressure Rice Cooker
body:
The CUCKOO CRP-JHR0609F is an exceptional 6-cup induction heating pressure rice cooker that brings both advanced technology and elegant design to your kitchen. This cooker, made in Korea, stands out with its sophisticated copper finish and robust functionality, making it a fantastic addition for any rice enthusiast.

One of the standout features of this rice cooker is its 13 menu options. Whether you're cooking white rice, brown rice, GABA rice, porridge, or even making a quick cook, this versatile machine handles it all with precision. The induction heating technology ensures even cooking, resulting in perfectly cooked rice every time. The pressure cooking feature further enhances the texture and flavor, giving you restaurant-quality results at home.

The auto-clean function is a huge time-saver, making maintenance a breeze. With just a touch of a button, the cooker cleans itself, ensuring hygiene and convenience. Additionally, the voice guide feature is particularly helpful, especially for those new to using advanced rice cookers. It provides clear instructions and feedback, available in multiple languages, making the cooking process straightforward and user-friendly.

The build quality of the CUCKOO CRP-JHR0609F is impressive, reflecting the high standards of Korean manufacturing. The materials used are durable and the design is both modern and aesthetically pleasing, fitting seamlessly into any kitchen decor.

In terms of capacity, the 6-cup (uncooked) size is perfect for small to medium-sized families, offering ample servings without taking up excessive counter space. The intuitive control panel and clear display further enhance the overall user experience, making this rice cooker easy to operate even for beginners.

Overall, the CUCKOO CRP-JHR0609F rice cooker is a high-performing, reliable, and stylish kitchen appliance. Its advanced features, ease of use, and excellent cooking results make it well worth the investment for anyone serious about their rice.

author: Pang Presa
title: I love rice!
body:
I'm one of those people that grew up with a rice cooker, but was never taught how it could be used it for more than just rice, it was just known and never acknowledged. Growing up, they were all pretty basic, to middle of the road, type of rice cookers, most of which have the electric plate heating and a variety of different types of stainless steel, aluminum, or non-stick coated pans.

I've always wanted one of those fancy rice cookers that talks, has all kinds of sound effects, music  and/or talks to you, and I grabbed this mostly because I wanted to see if there really is a big difference between the ones I've mentioned vs one that costs 3-5x more than some rice cookers, and has induction, and/or pressure cooking features.

Straight out of the box, it has this beautiful, brushed copper finish, black and silver details all around. On top of that it has backlit wording, a inset lit screen for the time notifications, lock and unlock dial, a pressure release valve and more. I greatly appreciate the fact that the inside plate on the top, as well as the pressure valve casing comes off, and there is a water dispenser on the back side , for easy cleaning. The cooking pot/bowl has sturdy plastic handles, which are easy to the touch when the rest of the pot is hot. The inside of the bowl is coated and has all kinds of indication lines for anything you can think of. Seriously, this thing is a tank and it's super bougie. Like so fancy, with so many details and features, I feel like I shouldn't have it in my possession.

My first dish would naturally be rice, to get a good baseline, but I decided to go hard and made Filipino porridge called Lugaw, which I normally cook on the stove in under an hour. I checked the recipe in the given manual, to get an idea of ratios needed and used that mostly as a guide since lugaw contains some other ingredients than a standard chicken porridge, plus I wanted to make double the amount. The measuring cup included, doesn't have ccs noted for liquid measure, so I had to do a quick conversion of 1.23cups, that equates to 300cc of water/broth. Thankfully the rice bowl also has liquid lines noted inside too, but I still felt like I had a little bit less water than I should've used. Either way, I set it all and forgot it. About an hour later, it sounded off like a choo choo, indicating it was releasing steam and soon let me know it was time. I opened up the rice cooker, and it was magic. I mixed everything around, everything was evenly cooked, and nothing was burned one bit! Did I need more liquid? Not really, the rice cooker just knew. I actually like my lugaw thicker, but could easily add more broth to make it a little lighter, thinner, and soupy.

Honestly, I've looked high and low, for videos and data on induction cooking rice makers like this and the reasons why this costs that much and I'm still trying to figure that out, as every video I saw gave the basics, and those on the tubes just made rice with no clear data, or idea on how to review a rice cooker. I'm not saying this will be #1 review, but I'm trying. The big things the company advertises is that this one provides a higher pressure than most, and it has induction heating, which ensures more even cooking. My mother is convinced that it eliminates starch, but that's a high claim and I'm not a believer in that so much, with any type of rice cooker. The options and guidance are definitely a big plus with this, and I plan on making it my right hand man in the kitchen next to the air fryer, since time and energy is so limited when it comes to making meals up to 2-3 times a day. On top of that, it makes just enough food for 2 people, and has some leftover for the next day compared to my slow cooker that can take all day, and up to 8 hours for one meal, and more leftovers than my freezer can handle!

Honestly, this guy is not necessary if you plan on using a rice cooker like this JUST to make rice, but I have seen lower level models with the same, or similar features from this company at big box warehouses. This is really the bougie version of certain models with all the fancy details, mechanics, and look. Plus it's a beast compared to my other 6 cup rice cooker, so you'll also have to accommodate for the size in your kitchen. Think deep, not wide. Either way, I'm totally keeping this since I plan to make it more of an everyday appliance, compared to my other rice cooker that just takes a nap in the cupboard and comes out to play once a week. Try it if you must, but know if you pay the price, appliances like these are more of an investment.

author: Amazon customer
title: The manual is confusing, disorganized and has tiny print but it makes great congee!
body:
The white rice is clumpy despite rinsing it until completely clear.  The brown rice was best but I realized I used the wrong water line and used less water.

I also made Gaba rice which turned out good, it was slightly clumpy although the texture was good after adding butter.  After some googling, I found out that after you soak the rice for 16 hours, the Gaba process sprouts the rice during a 2-hour process and the last hour cooks the rice.
But even the Gaba rice was slightly clumpy.  I did let the rice rest for 10 mins this time and it was better.

I had to start highlighting sections of the manual so I could find the scattered information.  Page 17 is very important because it is there that it tells you the water line to use for Brown Rice.  There is a small tidbit about the Direct Touch menus but there is no title to grab your attention and the print is so tiny it’s easy to miss.  There is no mention of the steam plate.

To start, there is a MODE button and a Selection dial and the voice helps you along, thankfully.  When you turn her on, she is speaking Korean, so I was in a bit of a panic but it was easy to use the Mode function to set to English AND to set the time.

I focused on cooking rice and ignored setting up timers for reheating and warming, and the My Mode feature, until I am comfortable with the settings.

I tested how well it cooks rice by making medium grain brown rice.  Each grain was perfectly cooked despite using less water.  Then I tried white jasmine rice, which turned out very clumpy, even though I had rinsed it until the water was super clear.

I wanted to use the steamer plate.  No where in the manual does it say anything about steaming.  There’s a Multi-Cook function but the only thing it mentions is how to change the preset time of the Multi-Cook function. I contacted support for this reason and they sent me a PDF manual that has a different recipe table than what is in the manual that came with my machine.  So again, the manual is lacking.

The 6-cup unit is a little over 14 inches in depth but the feet sit approximately 10 inches apart.  It’s not terribly heavy, so easy to move around.  The cord is located on the left side and fairly short.  The cup markings inside are white which makes them easy to see, which I love. One side is Korean, the other side is printed in English.

There is no way to turn off the unit, which bugs me but it does turn to power save mode

To make rice on any of the Direct Touch selections, merely add rice and then add water to the correct line and then touch your selection.  Brown rice you must also use the Gaba line. I’m a bit disappointed as I make better rice on the stove-top.  I am still researching to see if I'm missing something.

author: Ashley
title: Serious Safety Issue - Cannot Recommend
body:
I really wanted to love this cooker. It’s an aesthetically beautiful appliance and feels very well-built out of the box. The materials, finish, user interface, and overall design are impressive and give the feel of a premium product.

Unfortunately, that’s where the positives ended for me.

First, the cooker does not fully seal during operation, even when using pressure settings. According to the manufacturer (who I contacted after being concerned about the constant steam), some steam release during cooking is “normal,” but in normal use this means a constant stream of steam during the cooking cycle. This is not how most pressure cookers behave and requires you to be mindful of placement (e.g., near a vent or away from cabinets), which is not something I expected at this price point.

The bigger issue - and the reason I'm writing this review - is a safety concern I experienced while using the built-in quinoa function (a non-pressure cycle).

I followed the instructions exactly:

-Used the included measuring cup
-Filled to the indicated water line per the manual instructions
-Cooked a small batch (1 cup)
-Selected the correct, built in quinoa setting

During the cycle, the quinoa foamed and clogged the steam vent. Because the unit relies on that vent for steam release - even in a non-pressure cycle - pressure began to build inside the cooker. Eventually, the lid fully popped open.

This should not happen under any circumstances. Even if a food foams or clogs a vent, a pressure-capable appliance should have redundant safety mechanisms to prevent pressure buildup and keep the lid securely locked. The fact that the lid opened indicates a serious failure to safely manage internal pressure.

To be clear, this wasn’t a case of overfilling or using the wrong settings; I followed the instructions exactly, using a built-in program specifically intended for quinoa. That makes this particularly concerning and is a significant safety issue that could cause serious damage or injury.

At this price point, I expected a versatile, reliable multi-cooker. Instead, this feels like a very nice-looking, very expensive rice cooker with limited capability for anything beyond basic, low-foam foods. Given the serious safety concern I experienced, I cannot recommend it and will be returning mine.

author: huntinghawk
title: Makes good white rice
body:
I'm a third generation American of Japanese Ancestry pushing 60 years of age, and I've spent all my life eating white rice.  My mother taught me how to cook rice on a wood fire, for general knowledge, and I grew up on simple one button rice cookers that would shut off after the boiling stage, while the rice finished cooking by steaming on the residual heat, basically mimicking the open fire cooking method.

Growing up in the US, most white rice encountered in restaurants were disappointing, even in so called Japanese restaurants.  Many people don't soak the rice before cooking, and they use the knuckle measuring technique, often resulting in hard or mushy rice.

It is common knowledge that rice in Japan is better, primarily because of the quality of the rice.  In Hawaii, we buy relatively inexpensive rice grown in California.  So, it is important to use the best cooking methods to make the best of what we have in terms of rice.

The Cuckoo rice cooker is a pressure cooker, so the rice comes out with a nice shiny appearance and the grains hold their texture, i.e. not mushy.  It makes for very good and consistent rice.

But it is not perfect rice in my opinion.  The machine calls the white rice "glutinous" rice.  I think this means sticky, which it is.  It is a little too sticky for sushi rice for example.  Also, the rice has a slight dark tint, almost grey.  These are minor in my opinion, as I simply eat white rice like the way most Americans eat bread or pasta, and the Cuckoo machine does a fine job at cooking white rice for Asians like me.

title: Extremely Disappointing Product Quality and Customer Service
body:
I have purchased three Cuckoo rice cookers so far, and all of them failed within a year of use. For the first defective unit, I contacted the manufacturer hoping to get it repaired, but they wanted me to ship it to their U.S. service center which would cost over $200 for shipping alone. Adding the repair cost on top of that, it made more sense to just buy a new one rather than repair it. So I had to discard the faulty unit.

The second and third units faced the same issue of failing prematurely within a year. This time, I reached out to the Amazon seller for a replacement or refund, but they simply declined citing Amazon's 30-day return policy had lapsed, despite these being expensive $500 products. The seller showed absolutely no interest in making an exception or finding a solution - they just kept copy-pasting generic responses.

Not only did the product itself fail to last even a year despite its premium pricing, but the customer service from both the manufacturer and the seller was extremely poor. The manufacturer expected me to pay exorbitant shipping fees, and the seller outright refused any kind of make-good solution like a replacement or refund.

It is unacceptable for a $500 appliance to conk out within a year repeatedly. I have been forced to simply discard three faulty units without any resolution from either party. Prospective buyers, please beware and reconsider purchasing this terribly unreliable product with absolutely non-existent after-sales support.

My only gripe is that the LED screen has orange lights instead of the white as depicted in pictures which is why I demoted a star. author: AmazonCustomers
title: A Perfect Blend of Convenience and Quality
body:
I recently purchased the CUCKOO CRP-P0609S 6-cup pressure rice cooker, and I couldn't be happier with my decision. This rice cooker offers a fantastic blend of convenience and quality, which has made it an essential appliance in my kitchen.

The 12 menu options are a game-changer, allowing me to cook various types of rice and grains, including white, brown, and mixed rice, as well as porridge and soups. The intelligent cooking algorithm ensures that my rice is always cooked to perfection, with the right amount of moisture and texture.

The 6-cup capacity is ideal for my family, as it allows us to cook enough rice for multiple meals. The pressure cooking feature also speeds up the cooking process and helps preserve the nutritional value of the rice.

The design is sleek and modern, making it an attractive addition to my countertop. The easy-to-use LED screen and control panel make it simple to select the desired cooking mode and customize settings. The non-stick inner pot is easy to clean, and the safety features, such as the pressure control and automatic steam release, give me peace of mind while using the appliance.

In summary, the CUCKOO CRP-P0609S pressure rice cooker has exceeded my expectations and made cooking rice a breeze. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a reliable and high-quality rice cooker that offers both convenience and versatility.

body: Thought I was getting a high end rice cooker, however, got a expensive low end rice cooker. Apparently, you are not supposed to wash the rice inside the non-stick cooking pot, because it will scratch the non-stick coating inside.  The user interface is not user friendly, with buttons spread through out the front of the rice cooker interface.  Don't know why there is a lock and unlock (which you have to turn to lock/unlock) feature on the rice cooker, I've never seen that on any other rice cooker.  Thought this rice cooker would be able to make nurungji / crispy - crunchy rice, however it does not work, unless you cook your rice in the nurungji function 3 to 4 times, which takes 3-4 hours.  Otherwise, this is an average rice cooker, which needs a lot of improvements to justify the hefty price.

author: Paul Goodman
title: Not good for brown rice or basmati rice. Pressure cooking is a bad idea for rice.
body:
After lots of experience with many rice cookers, my requirements for a rice cooker were pretty basic: it must not burn itself up due to faulty electronics, it must not have a potentially toxic Teflon or similar nonstick pot, and it must make decent brown rice. This Cuckoo had some great reviews on various sites, so I splurged and tried it. Big mistake! Now it's too late to return it.

The first thing you notice is that it TALKS TO YOU! Loudly. And it talks in Korean. It's unnecessarily difficult to turn off the talking function. The instruction manual is unclear and hard to understand, and turning off the talking is completely non-obvious; it took a while.

The big issue is that pressure cooking is simply a bad idea for cooking rice if you don't want it to be sticky and mushy. Non-pressurized cooking works much better. At first, I followed the instructions for brown rice and it came out awfully gooey and sticky. Yuk! I experimented with different water to rice ratios and found that 1.25 to 1, or even 1 to 1, is about right. But still, the rice is never as good as it should be. Soaking the rice before heating doesn't help. I also tried this with basmati rice, and had more problems - almost inedible. It just doesn't work well.

The instructions are awful. There are some tantalizing options for "preset" and "multi-cook", but they don't help, and there is zero useful information about them in the user manual.

And, this machine is big - it takes up a lot of counter space. Not good.

On the plus side, it seems to be quite well designed and made, after you get over the basic problems of functionality. The pot interior has an "X-well Diamond" coating, which somewhat resembles the nonstick diamond surface of Swiss Diamond pans, which are excellent (and very expensive). I like that part.

Eventually, I found another rice cooker that actually does meet the basic requirements, as far as I can tell: the Instant Pot Zest https://www.amazon.com/Instant-Zest-Rice-Cooker-Pot/dp/B07TZL8Y3C/. For about $40, you get a NON pressurized rice cooker, which is exactly what you need to make great rice, a ceramic lined nonstick pot, and (according to the manufacturer) overheat sensing, which should prevent overheating and burning. It's pretty small on the counter, and quite simple to use. The small (8 cup) model is more than sufficient for a family of 4.

About overheating: I have had TWO Aroma rice cookers fail by overheating to the point that they created large amounts of horrible smoke and might have caught fire if I hadn't unplugged them. I even had the US Consumer Product Safety Commission investigate the first one. No surprise, they never got back to me and did not stop Aroma from selling those defective devices. Some other low price rice cookers have similar complaints from users. Buyer beware!

And, no, I will not use a rice cooker with PFOA, PFAS, or any other sort of Teflon-related non-stick liner. Note that even the very expensive Zojirushi rice cookers use those substances, and many users complain about the nonstick stuff flaking off. Not for my family!

author: Brandon E.
title: All flash, no intuition.
body:
This rice cooker failed to do the little things well, while making good rice. But not 300$ good rice.

My perspective is that I am a decent cook, I like simplicity and intuitive design. I make rice maybe 3 times a week.

Size:
This rice cooker is way too big for its job. I'm an American so the rice cooker isn't the center of my kitchen. It's another tool I take out of the cabinet. This rice cooker would have to sit on my counter taking up space unused for most of the week.

Software:
The standard language is Korean. Although you can set it to English, the 300$ machine has no non-volitile memory. Meaning that when you unplug it and put it away, it will talk to you in Korean when you plug it in in a few days. I'm an American who eats rice every once in a while and I don't intend to have this rice cooker plugged in forever like a microwave.

For the buyer:
Other than these simple oversights, the rice cooker does cook a pretty good pot of rice. But not anything that a 100$ cooker couldn't.

For the Manufacturer:
This would be a fantastic rice cooker for Korean buyers. If you'd like to enter the American market, consider designing the dimensions so the rice cooker can be stowed in a cabinet. And if the product has a North American electrical socket, the standard language should be set to English. These small oversights make this product difficult to live with.

author: DG
title: Nice price, but not sure it was completely new...
body:
The way the box came with one loose box strap/band way over to a side, tape on top of box seal looked possibly tampered with, and the electric cord wrapping was loose, messy and uneven as though someone had undone the wire tie, then re-wrapped it.  But we looked the machine over, and it seemed clean, so we set it up and tried it.  First water boil test to check seals took 3 tries to get it work (chalked it up to likely operator error...) and steam came out the way it was supposed to - just through the steam vent.  I let Amazon know, and they offered to replace/refund, but we decided we'd try it for a week, and then see.  (Sort of a gift for Mom, so wanted her to feel good about a new rice cooker.)
We started noticing the lid latch didn't always release easily - would take a few attempts.  After about 3 or 4 days, we noticed the outer bottom of the inner pot had an area that had already worn, like it had been rubbed hard and some of the finishing was 'off', size of a quarter, (like a scratched teflon pan), but we'd been very careful not to scratch or ding it, so not sure why.  Decided there were enough questionable things that I called in to Amazon.  They promptly sent a replacement.  We got it yesterday, and comparing it to the first, the 2nd's vent cover - internal area had what looked like a couple of oil stains on the silicone seal - I could excuse it as possibly a test that they did, and it washed off.  The steam pressure weight has a burnt discolored looking area near the inner circle - chalking it up to manufacturing - too tired to clean off another one and go through returns.  But comparing it against the first, the inside of this weight is clean, the first is black inside (q-tip brings off some carbon from the 1st weight.  Not sure that just a week of making rice in the first should do that, but we'll check this 2nd one after a week of making rice.  BIG difference.  1st cooker made the Calrose (short-grain sushi rice) EXTRA sticky, like glutinous mochi rice.  definitely a lot stickier than we'd expected, but we figured that must be the way it works.  We have a really old Cuckoo that's been working, just the inner lid isn't removeable, and it's started to wear, so figured it was time for a new one, and that didn't make rice this sticky.  Well, this 2nd one makes the rice much closer to the old Cuckoo (SRP-0611FA).  So maybe the first CRP-P0609S does have something wrong with it? Or maybe this 2nd one has something wrong with it? Have no idea at this point.
1. Inner pot site description says stainless steel.  This is more like aluminum, and doesn't feel like anodized just b/c of the weight - at least my anodized aluminum pots are much heavier for a similar size.
2. I'd personally like to upgrade a step or two, but Mom likes the darker color and doesn't feel like it's worth paying more (not her money, but that's just family dynamics...)
- Might update this after we've used the replacement for a bit, but hoping there won't be any issues or questions with this one...

Used almost everyday. Also super easy to clean and like a car, you must keep it clean for a long lasting supply of delicious rice, which is super easy bc its mostly just wiping the inside and clearing it of dropped rice grains, ensuring the rubber does not produce mold.. Most satisfied investment in food products to buy.

title: Don??t go for it if you expected a high quality Japanese rice cooker, they are just not the same.
body: Well, this is my first time to write any product review from my Amazon purchase.  The product earned 2 out of 5 stars across various categories, are pretty much to it failed to meet with my expectations.  I grow up in a traditional Asian family where rice cooker is one of the most important cooking tools in the kitchen.  I have to admit that my family and I are pretty ??serious?? on the type of rice we eat, as well as how the rice cooker could perform.  With a so-called ??smart-rice cooker?? at this price point, all I could say is that IT COULD NOT COOK THE RICE THAT I EXPECTED. No matter which programme I choose, or the amount of water I added, the rice was never soft enough. Compared to my TIGER brand $99 from Costco, this $360 Made in Korea rice cooker just can??t even make a decent porridge.  All I presume is the programme and the high pressure technology could have two advantages. One, quick that I could have my rice done in about 20 minutes. Two, the steam and high pressure is good with the grain rice.Unfortunately, this pricy rice cooker (probably because it was invented and branded from Korean) didn??t have the receipt for the rice to sit enough time to absorb enough water.  In the due course, the rice is for those who like ??harder??.Last but least, when look into details, many plastic parts including the attached accessories are flimsy.  All I could say ??don??t go for it if you expected to have a high quality Japanese rice cooker??, they are just not the same.

date: Reviewed in the United States on September 10, 2020
author: Koala Balla
title: Best rice cooker I've used
body: This is my first time purchasing a Cuckoo rice cooker and I'm extremely impressed. There are some minor caveats/things to bear in mind when you buy this, but TL;DR: this is a solid rice cooker and I haven't made better rice with any other rice cooker.First, the design is sleak -- the back w/ rose gold goes well with most of our appliances, and adds a nice bit of accent color to the kitchen. My only complaint about the external design is how thin some of the platic feels to the touch. This doesn't 'feel' like a product in its price point; it feels much cheaper. I could imagine this breaking irreparably if dropped.The built-in voices are fun -- being greeted with a little jingle and hearing a voice notify me of each stage of the cooking process is really nice, in spite of being more of a 'fun' thing than a practical one. The voice is in multiple languages, and can be disabled entirely. Again, a bit over-the-top, but it has its function of offering me the freedom to work about the kitchen without constantly checking the rice cooker.This particular rice cooker is non-stick while avoiding the use of teflon. I do not have burnt rice stuck on the bottom of the bowl -- instead, I get consistent rice to my liking from top to bottom, and I don't need to worry about chips of teflon in my food.It has a self-sanitizing feature, that will use hot water to sanitize itself. It should be noted the self-sanitizing is not self-cleaning. In other words, you still need to detach the various plates and components to sufficiently clean the unit. One should not rely on this feature alone to keep their rice cooker clean and in good condition.Speaking of components, there are multiple components that are detachable for cleaning purposes, specifically in the lid. This is a pressure rice cooker, and the various lids and steam filters need cleaning. This is fine and dandy, but the first plate in the lid really requires some strength. It is held in by a thick rubber gromet with a tiny rubber handle, which you can pull to remove the plate. The rubber handle is small and smooth, so people with big fingers/hands will struggle getting a decent grip on it, and people with smaller fingers and hand may struggle with the amount of force required to detach it.It is areas in the design like this and the plastic enclosure where cuckoo made clear design decisions to save on production costs. Luckily, none of these things detract from the quality of the product it yields.I have NEVER cooked better straight rice out of the rice cooker than I have with this.There are several cooking modes to choose from -- most folks will use the glutinous rice setting, which has 3 settings of its own - normal, high heat, and turbo.Normal mode will cook the rice in around 40 minutesHigh heat will cook the rice in about 30Turbo will cook it in about 20The quality degrades the higher power you use -- but not by much. The worst 'quality' rice I got was using the turbo setting for glutinous rice -- it was only slightly tougher than what I'd have preferred, but if I'm in a pinch for time, the turbo mode yields rice that is good enough.Normal mode seems to have the best yield, as the rice is evenly cooked from top to bottom. There are zero 'hard' pieces of rice, nor a collection of burnt rice on the bottom of the bowl, reducing waste. Each grain is soft and is as sticky as I want.It's important to note there are timed modes, as well as ways to customize each option's cook settings, so you can tweak the presets to suit your needs.All in all, this is one of the best cooking appliances I've purchased in awhile.

author: M. Smith
title: Easy to use, but make sure you follow instructions
body:
This rice cooker makes great rice, it cooks quickly, and thoroughly, and is the most similar to cooking rice on the stove than other rice cookers I've tried. I do add a little extra water than the fill lines recommend to achieve that stickier texture, but it works well without being mushy or soggy.

The only issue I've had with this rice cooker is that the removeable silicone ring on the lid has to be placed exactly in the correct position, or else it will not allow the steam to be released properly.

There is a removeable part of the lid that has a silicone ring on it that can be removed for cleaning, but after that is removed, there is a separate silicone ring attached to the lid itself that can be removed for cleaning. I popped it back on after cleaning and noticed that the next time I cooked rice, the water leaked out from the handles. When I looked it up online, I realized that I had installed that ring incorrectly, and there are markings that have to line up or else it won't function properly.

As long as everything is reinstalled on the cooker properly after cleaning, it's fine, but you just have to be certain to line everything up properly.

body:
I think this rice cooker is just okay. There's a lot of inconsistencies in the rice results...and if you eat a lot of Jasmin rice, I don't think it is the best cooker for that. It does very well for brown and GABA rice, and short grain. It doesn't do well for that special crunchy bottom rice, which is more chewy than crunchy, and I think not good for my teeth enamel. The pressure unit doesn't seem to work properly. It originally would be silent when cooking, until the pressure release, but now it just cooks with the release valve pretty much open on its own. The inside steel plate that's removable for cleaning has a super short silicone that makes it difficult remove without using a dry cloth for gripping. This same plate also falls into the rice while cooking pretty regularly, so I think that silicone gasket that secures it isn't right during cooking. I hate opening up my rice cooker to see this plate sitting directly on top of my rice. There's many little annoying features that just don't work. I also hate it when my rice turns out grey. It only does it sometimes, so I am not sure why. Maybe I don't wash the rice enough. But I have never had grey rice with any other cooker in my entire life of rice cooking. So I get worried about the chemicals that might be in my grey rice.

I have had this cooker for over a month now, and compared to my old fuzzy logic Zojirushi rice cooker, I find the rice better with my old cooker. The good thing about the newer Cuckoo is the speed , and it cooks a good brown and GABA rice much better because of the high pressure. But we don't eat brown that often.

I am contemplating on replacing this with a Zojirushi again, and saving this for when I need to make brown rice. Pretty disappointing overall. The Cuckoo does the two things better that my old cooker lacked, but I don't know if it was enough to sacrifice for quality, white (not grey) rice.

Press 'Auto Clean'  one time to enter changing mode2. Press and hold 'Auto Clean' 3 secs to enter voice change in language. You will see the flashing of '0:  0', which is current setting in Korean voice3. Press 'Menu >' to change from '0:  0' to '0:  1'  for English voice. Now you will hear voice in English.4. Press 'Pressure Cook/ Glutin Turbo'  to save and exit.  Done!

I also used the multi function frequently and cook chicken, pork chop with onions and garlic.  It tasted really delicious.  The onions melt into a sauce within 45 min of Multi Cook function.  The auto clean button is a life saver.  I used the cooker to cook fish before, it tasted good but left a bad smell afterward.  The auto clean is really easy to use, you pour water up to the 2 cups line and the cooker would auto clean/sterilize for you. After it runs its cycle, any stains can be wipe out clean easily.  This is my first Cuckoo and I highly recommend it.  The black color also makes it look very classy in the kitchen.  It also speaks English and Korean.  It will tell you when it is several minutes away from done cooking.  My daughter also used it to make a cake with the recipe included.  It was a little dry but still tasted good. Love it!

title: huntinghawk
body: yes
style: I'm a third generation American of Japanese Ancestry pushing 60 years of age, and I've spent all my life eating white rice.  My mother taught me how to cook rice on a wood fire, for general knowledge, and I grew up on simple one button rice cookers that would shut off after the boiling stage, while the rice finished cooking by steaming on the residual heat, basically mimicking the open fire cooking method.Growing up in the US, most white rice encountered in restaurants were disappointing, even in so called Japanese restaurants.  Many people don't soak the rice before cooking, and they use the knuckle measuring technique, often resulting in hard or mushy rice.It is common knowledge that rice in Japan is better, primarily because of the quality of the rice.  In Hawaii, we buy relatively inexpensive rice grown in California.  So, it is important to use the best cooking methods to make the best of what we have in terms of rice.The Cuckoo rice cooker is a pressure cooker, so the rice comes out with a nice shiny appearance and the grains hold their texture, i.e. not mushy.  It makes for very good and consistent rice.But it is not perfect rice in my opinion.  The machine calls the white rice "glutinous" rice.  I think this means sticky, which it is.  It is a little too sticky for sushi rice for example.  Also, the rice has a slight dark tint, almost grey.  These are minor in my opinion, as I simply eat white rice like the way most Americans eat bread or pasta, and the Cuckoo machine does a fine job at cooking white rice for Asians like me.

style: I have purchased three Cuckoo rice cookers so far, and all of them failed within a year of use. This time, I reached out to the Amazon seller for a replacement or refund, but they simply declined citing Amazon's 30-day return policy had lapsed, despite these being expensive $500 products. The seller showed absolutely no interest in making an exception or finding a solution - they just kept copy-pasting generic responses.Not only did the product itself fail to last even a year despite its premium pricing, but the customer service from both the manufacturer and the seller was extremely poor. author: John Book
title: Fast, Powerful, and Thoughtfully Designed — A Big Upgrade from Zojirushi
body:
I’ve used a Zojirushi rice cooker for over eight years, so switching brands wasn’t a light decision. After using the CUCKOO High Pressure Rice Cooker, I can confidently say this was one of the best kitchen upgrades I’ve ever made.

⸻

What I Like

The most impressive feature is how fast it cooks. Rice is ready in about 20 minutes, which is a huge improvement compared to my old cooker. Despite the speed, the quality doesn’t suffer at all. The high-pressure cooking produces rice that’s evenly cooked, fluffy, and well-textured.

Another major plus is the nonstick inner pot without Teflon. That was very important to me, and CUCKOO delivers here. Cleaning is easy, and I feel better knowing it avoids traditional Teflon coatings.

Performance-wise, it handles both short-grain and long-grain rice beautifully without compromise. Whether it’s sticky rice or regular long-grain, the results are consistently excellent.

The design also deserves praise. It looks modern, sleek, and premium—something you don’t mind leaving out on the countertop. It genuinely stands out compared to more utilitarian-looking rice cookers.

⸻

What Could Be Better

While the cooker performs extremely well, the interface and settings may take some time to get used to, especially if you’re coming from a simpler model. A clearer or more intuitive menu could improve the experience for first-time users.

Additionally, the price point may feel high upfront, though the performance and durability help justify the investment over time.

⸻

Overall Impression

The CUCKOO High Pressure Rice Cooker outperforms my long-trusted Zojirushi in speed, design, and cooking technology. Fast cooking, excellent results, a Teflon-free nonstick pot, and a standout design make this a top-tier rice cooker. Highly recommended for anyone serious about rice and willing to invest in quality.

I selected this model over the CRP-RT0609FW because it was going to be the same price and I liked the look of this one better. My top choice was CRP-LHTR0609FW but I didn't want to spend over $200. I had a Cuckoo 6 cup rice cooker from Korea that lasted nearly 15 years and used it at least 2-3 times per week. (We did use a step-down converter with it to use in the US and we had to replace the converter around the 10 year mark during this time). This one works like our old one and my kid loves the voice navigation function of our old one so we made sure to get one with it. The rice does seem to cook much faster. I would say my old one cooked in 30 minutes and this one does it in about 15-20 minutes. My only gripe is that the LED screen has orange lights instead of the white as depicted in pictures which is why I demoted a star. But if you watch videos or view actual images of this product when powered on, you will see that the display is orange. I don't regret my purchase because I got it for a deal of a price.

author: Hau L.
title: Poor Quality & Zero Accountability – Avoid This Brand!
body:
I purchased this Cuckoo pressure rice cooker in February 2022, and the inner pot started peeling within months. The coating didn’t just chip—it peeled off completely, making the pot look disgusting and unsafe. Check my attached photos; this is what you’ll be dealing with sooner or later.
When I contacted Cuckoo America, their response was shocking:
“The inner pot is considered a consumable part… not covered under warranty… please buy a replacement from our website.”
Translation? They expect the pot to fail and want you to keep paying for replacements. This is not normal wear and tear—it’s a design flaw and a quality failure. A premium rice cooker should last years without the inner pot disintegrating.
If you value durability and customer support, do NOT buy this product. Cuckoo refuses to stand behind their own product. Unless you’re okay with spending extra every few years for parts, look elsewhere. There are better brands that actually care about quality and customers.

author: Jorn Haagen
title: One 'sticky' trick pony....
body: If I hadn't found one for under half price here on Amazon, I'd given it two stars. Living in an apartment for 6 months, needing a rice cooker, I couldn't justify shelling out over $370 for a Zojirushi induction rice cooker as I already invested in one back at my house. If you have not used a Zojirushi, I guess a Cuckoo will be ok. But once you have gotten used to what the Zojirushi can do (especially the Umami setting), this just doesn't cut it. It does not matter how much you reduce the amount of water, this just does not want to do 'fluffy - 'dry' rice' no matter what brand Basmati you use. Sure, you can leave it to dry out over night, which works for fried rice, but this machine seems to be a one trick 'sticky-rice' pony. Is it worth its asking price, if you ask me, not even close. But if sticky is how you like ALL your rice, Basmati included, I'm sure this will satisfy plenty.

style: Thought I was getting a high end rice cooker, however, got a expensive low end rice cooker.  The non-stick cooking pot coating scratches very easily, which shouldn't happen in this high end price range. The user interface is not user friendly, with buttons spread through out the front of the rice cooker interface.  Don't know why there is a lock and unlock (which you have to turn to lock/unlock) feature on the rice cooker, I've never seen that on any other rice cooker.  Thought this rice cooker would be able to make nurungji / crispy - crunchy rice, however it does not work, unless you cook your rice in the nurungji function 3 to 4 times, which takes 3-4 hours. author: Hope Kang
title: Reliable, High-Quality Rice Cooker—Great Upgrade!
body:
Overall ★★★★★
Effectiveness ★★★★★
Price ★★★★☆
Safe ★★★★★
Re-purchase? Yes

After using the previous version of this rice cooker for over 10 years, it finally gave out due to a sensor issue. Since I’ve always trusted the quality and reasonable pricing of Korean rice cookers, I started searching for a similar model online. Luckily, I found this newer version of the one I previously owned.

First Impression:
One thing I realized after ordering was that my old rice cooker was a 5-cup model, but this one is a 10-cup size—so it’s much bigger than I expected! (A quick tip: always double-check the size before ordering to avoid the same mistake I made!) That said, the sleek white design of this rice cooker looks modern and blends well with my kitchen.

Performance:
As expected, this rice cooker delivered excellent results. I’ve used it to cook rice with beans and harder grains, and it cooked everything thoroughly and to perfection. The warming function works without any issues, keeping the rice at an ideal temperature. My family and I have been enjoying great meals since purchasing it, and we are fully satisfied.

Pros:

Excellent cooking performance
Modern and stylish design
Cons:

The size was bigger than anticipated (my mistake for not checking!)

body: yes
style: This rice cooker failed to do the little things well, while making good rice. But not 300$ good rice.My perspective is that I am a decent cook, I like simplicity and intuitive design. I make rice maybe 3 times a week.Size:This rice cooker is way too big for its job. I'm an American so the rice cooker isn't the center of my kitchen. It's another tool I take out of the cabinet. This rice cooker would have to sit on my counter taking up space unused for most of the week.Software:The standard language is Korean. Although you can set it to English, the 300$ machine has no non-volitile memory. Meaning that when you unplug it and put it away, it will talk to you in Korean when you plug it in in a few days. I'm an American who eats rice every once in a while and I don't intend to have this rice cooker plugged in forever like a microwave.For the buyer:Other than these simple oversights, the rice cooker does cook a pretty good pot of rice. But not anything that a 100$ cooker couldn't.For the Manufacturer:This would be a fantastic rice cooker for Korean buyers. If you'd like to enter the American market, consider designing the dimensions so the rice cooker can be stowed in a cabinet. And if the product has a North American electrical socket, the standard language should be set to English. These small oversights make this product difficult to live with.

style: Well, this is my first time to write any product review from my Amazon purchase.  The product earned 2 out of 5 stars across various categories, are pretty much to it failed to meet with my expectations.  I grow up in a traditional Asian family where rice cooker is one of the most important cooking tools in the kitchen.  I have to admit that my family and I are pretty ??serious?? on the type of rice we eat, as well as how the rice cooker could perform.  With a so-called ??smart-rice cooker?? at this price point, all I could say is that IT COULD NOT COOK THE RICE THAT I EXPECTED. No matter which programme I choose, or the amount of water I added, the rice was never soft enough. Compared to my TIGER brand $99 from Costco, this $360 Made in Korea rice cooker just can??t even make a decent porridge.  All I presume is the programme and the high pressure technology could have two advantages. One, quick that I could have my rice done in about 20 minutes. Two, the steam and high pressure is good with the grain rice.Unfortunately, this pricy rice cooker (probably because it was invented and branded from Korean) didn??t have the receipt for the rice to sit enough time to absorb enough water.  In the due course, the rice is for those who like ??harder??.Last but least, when look into details, many plastic parts including the attached accessories are flimsy.  All I could say ??don??t go for it if you expected to have a high quality Japanese rice cooker??, they are just not the same.
